messages.subject_clean: Testing the significance of factor loadings
messages.body_plain:
It seems a little silly to do this. The significance of the factor loadings is really the same as the significance of the slope parameters. They become slightly different if you are testing a value other than 0, in which case applying the delta method is possible but still not very recommended (I've written about this in a paper that studied profile-likelihood CIs, and these functions incidentally ended up into the function PLCI.mirt()). I would probably just report the significance of the raw slope parameters instead since this implies the significance of the loadings. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Tuning setting of MHRM algorithm
messages.subject_clean: Tuning setting of MHRM algorithm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sebastian,

The stochastic integration in the MHRM algorithm effectively solves the problem of numerical integration for you at the cost of slower convergence to the point MLE estimates. So long as the acceptance rates are reasonable, such as between .3-.7, then the space should be sufficiently sampled to deal with the integration problem. If not, that's when some tuning is going to be required, though more recent versions of mirt now try to calculate better candidate draw perturbation values to make this more automatic throughout the estimation.

Of note that, with a very high-dimensional model there is a chance that the latent covariance matrix will become non-positive definite, which will result in problem and early termination. I have some plans to incorporate more robust variants for this, such as reparameterizing to use a Cholesky decomposition if the cov matrix instead, but this is lower on the TODO list since I don't believe it as flexible when specifying the model. HTH.

Phil

Hi Christoph,

I don't think that such recommendations exist since there are a lot of moving pieces to work with. The test length, type of item, number of response categories, magnitude of the IRT parameters, underlying theta distribution, and so on, all play a part in the power computations; so, overall it's quite difficult to tell. The more individuals collected the better, and for the 2PL you could get away with fewer. The only way to really tell is via simulations that focus on the output statistics you're interested in (e.g., power/Type I errors, stability of parameter estimates, etc). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Second order test in mixedmirt function
messages.body_plain:
Someone also raised this issue recently, and I believe it is an artifact of Cai's approach to estimating the ACOV. The MHRM method effectively jitters the parameter estimates around the MLE estimates and computes the gradient/Hessian of the complete data solution to form the observed information/ACOV estimate. However, because the MLEs are being jittered there can be some over/underinflation effects, where even unidentified models could appear identified if the stochastic parameters are in a more 'curved' location. Hence, as it turns out, the MHRM ACVOV approach is rather poor at detecting non-identified models.

The better approach is the use the 'FMHRM' method, which fixes the values at the MLE rather than allowing them to jump around, and gives a Monte Carlo estimate at that location instead. I've found this is much more stable/reasonable, but the cost right now is that it takes longer to compute (it could likely be parallelized though, and when that gets implemented I'll no doubt make the default for the MHRM the 'FMHRM' method instead to avoid problems like this). HTH you understand the issue a little better.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This is my first message... I have been getting familiar with IRT and Mirt, and I am actually quite excited. So, thanks to all of you.

Now, to my question.
I am trying to develop a scale that measures "comfort" (I am not going to provide any other irrelevant details).
This will be measured by means of Bipolar Adjective Rating Scales (i.e. Likert Scales)
I expect these items to have different difficulties;
maybe no one will answer "Very much agree" to the hardest item,
maybe no one will say "very much disagree" to the easiest one.
The data that I am really interested in is the difficulty and discrimination of each item (i.e. I need to leave the slope unconstrained)

So, I have been simulating data by faking some Generalized Parcial Credit Model items

theta <- runif(n_observations, min_theta, max_theta)
sim_data <- simdata(discriminations, intercepts, Theta=matrix(theta), itemtype="gpcm")

and then fitting by using GRSM and grsmIRT models.

results <- mirt(data = this_data, model=1, itemtype="grsmIRT", SE=TRUE)

Now, I am getting the error message of

Error: Graded rating scale models require items to have the same number of categories

So, I have searched (I found THIS <https://github.com/philchalmers/mirt/issues/158>, for instance, and some other sources), but I am not really sure what to do in the end.

I know collapsing responses is an option but, wouldn't that affect the real "difficulty" of an item? I mean, is this fair for the "difficult items" to just say "Oh, you are just like the one next to you". My point is that this feel like a violation to the model of this item
Should I choose a different item type? Which one is recommended? (I tried "gpcm", but I think it has too many moving parts, and I got high p-values a lot of the times)
Why do rated models need observed data in ALL categories? Can't they just try to fit by using "Zero" in some observed frequencies?
Finally: Any suggestion on the best way to measure the Goodness-Of-Fit? I understand chi-squared tends to overreject when expected frequencies are low (which is, I think, what happened to me when using gpcm model).
Thanks very much! I will create another question with different doubts.

Cheers,

messages.subject: Re: Bifactor Question
messages.subject_clean: Bifactor Question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gene,

the answer is yes, the main factor will be biased. Another interpretation is, that the main factor is only interpretable relative to an item set and is not an absolute property of an item. I do not have a nice reference for this, but we ran some simulations a while ago and analysed some data from another personality scale (coincidentally also neuroticism).

How large the bias is, will depend on the ratio of the items, their variances and their intercorrelations. The easiest way I found to look into this is to resample items or systematically vary the ratio. The correlation of the main factor with the anxiety items will increase as their number increases. As a consequence I believe scale construction needs to make sure a priori that facets are equally well represented in the item set.

Kind wishes,
Philipp (Doebler)

messages.subject_clean: Why negative discrimination value using exploratory mirt
messages.body_plain:
It's probably best that you look up linear exploratory factor analysis first, which is the traditional factor analysis using correlation matricies. IRT's exploratory factor analysis is effectively the same, except that dependent variables are modeled as categorical data rather than continuous. The answer to you question is that the coefficients extracted are maximally saturated in that they are only unique up to linear transformations, so negative values appear to reflect this level of saturation. Hence, you would need rotations to find a better orientation, and ideally this solution provides information as to a more constrained 'confirmatory' factor analytic model in the future. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Germán,

I just noticed this email in my spam folder; no sure why it went there as most messages from the forum come through fine. Below are my responses to your questions.

>
> I know collapsing responses is an option but, wouldn't that affect the real "difficulty" of an item? I mean, is this fair for the "difficult items" to just say "Oh, you are just like the one next to you". My point is that this feel like a violation to the model of this item

Correct, collapsing categories is probably not what you want and should only be done for practical ad-hoc reasons (like difficulty in estimating extreme parameters).

> Should I choose a different item type? Which one is recommended? (I tried "gpcm", but I think it has too many moving parts, and I got high p-values a lot of the times)

The gpcm is probably a good place to start anyway as this is the more general version of the rating scale models. If these fit well then you can turn to a more constrained variant to see if imposing further constraints does not negatively affect the precision of the model too much.

> Why do rated models need observed data in ALL categories? Can't they just try to fit by using "Zero" in some observed frequencies?

The issue has to do with parameterization. How does mirt know how many parameters to use in each category if no hard-rule is set? E.g., if you have an item that has five distinct responses, but technically could have had up to 10 or 15 unique responses, how should the model be setup and estimated? How would I know that the observations were missing in the first place? You can somewhat trick mirt into thinking there are more categories via the customK input to the technical list, but be sure to inspect the starting values first to see if this is really what you are after.

> Finally: Any suggestion on the best way to measure the Goodness-Of-Fit? I understand chi-squared tends to overreject when expected frequencies are low (which is, I think, what happened to me when using gpcm model).

Functions like M2(), itemfit(), and residuals() are a good place to start. HTH.

Phil
